description.en: A single vowel mark at the end of a word can change the meaning of a whole sentence. This lesson covers what the science of nahw (Arabic grammar) is, what it is for, how it began, and its best-known schools, scholars and books.

description.ar:
ما الكلامُ عند النحاة؟ وما الذي يجعل الجملة «مفيدة»؟
في هذا الدرس: تعريف الكلام بقيوده الأربعة (اللفظ، المركّب، المفيد، الوضع)، ثم أقسامه الثلاثة: الاسم وأنواعه، والفعل وأقسامه، والحرف بين حروف المباني وحروف المعاني، مع تطبيقٍ على نصٍّ لابن قتيبة من مقدّمة «أدب الكاتب».

description.en: What counts as speech (kalam) for the Arabic grammarians, and what makes a sentence meaningful? This lesson covers the definition of kalam and its four conditions (uttered, compound, meaningful, by convention), then its three parts: the noun and its types, the verb and its categories, and the particle — letters of construction versus letters of meaning — with an applied reading of a passage by Ibn Qutayba from the introduction to Adab al-Katib.

description.en: How do you know a word is a noun? Is the ta in «حضرتُ» a noun? This lesson covers the five signs of the noun that Ibn Malik gathered in a single line of verse: the genitive (jarr), tanwin, the vocative, the definite article «أل», and predication (isnad) — any one of them is enough to identify a noun.

description.en: A single verb such as «كَتَبَ» carries six descriptions at once: past, sound, bare triliteral, transitive, active voice, and fully conjugable. This lesson covers the categories of the verb by tense, inflection and indeclinability, sound and weak roots, bare and augmented forms, intransitive and transitive, active and passive voice, and frozen versus conjugable verbs.

description.en: «ليسَ العلمُ بضارٍّ»: is «ضارٍّ» simply a genitive noun and nothing more? This lesson covers the Arabic prepositions (huruf al-jarr), Ibn Malik's two lines of verse that gather all twenty of them, the meanings of the most common ones, how a preposition carries the verb's meaning to the noun, their three types — original, redundant and quasi-redundant — and the i'rab of a noun governed by a redundant preposition.
